item.title: Autapse-inspired neuromorphic hardware with synapse–neuron integration for bidirectional feedback control
item.dc:creator: Chan Kim
Seonkwon Kim
Jeong Hwan Song
Jongyoung Lee
Leejae Kim
Seongil Im
Hyunsu Ju
Yoon Seok Jung
item.description:
Authors: Chan Kim, Seonkwon Kim, Jeong Hwan Song, Jongyoung Lee, Leejae Kim, Seongil Im, Hyunsu Ju, Yoon Seok Jung, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Establishing autonomous and energy-efficient feedback control at the hardware level remains challenging because conventional systems rely on centralized processing and continuous external computation, increasing energy consumption and system complexity. Here we show a neuromorphic autapse-inspired system that enables localized and bidirectional feedback control, using thermoregulation as a representative application. An autapse is a self-synaptic connection in which a neuron feeds its output back to its own synaptic input, enabling intrinsic feedback modulation. The system integrates a solid electrolyte-based synaptic transistor capable of multiplexing multiple inputs and a bidirectional leaky integrate-and-fire artificial neuron. By feeding the neuronal output back to an additional synaptic gate, excitatory and inhibitory feedback loops are realized within a compact architecture. Using an artificial thermoregulation platform, temperature-dependent inputs bidirectionally modulate neuronal firing frequency, demonstrating biologically inspired feedback control with a compact set of neuromorphic devices for autonomous and energy-efficient systems.

item.title: Scaling medical imaging report generation with multimodal reinforcement learning
item.dc:creator: Qianchu Liu
Sheng Zhang
Guanghui Qin
Yu Gu
Ying Jin
Sam Preston
Yanbo Xu
Sid Kiblawi
item.description:
Authors: Qianchu Liu, Sheng Zhang, Guanghui Qin, Yu Gu, Ying Jin, Sam Preston, Yanbo Xu, Sid Kiblawi, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract In medical imaging report generation, supervised fine-tuning can overfit to superficial patterns and generalize poorly across institutions. We introduce Universal Report Generation (UNIRG), which adopts reinforcement learning to directly optimize clinically meaningful quality criteria. With this framework, we developed UNIRG-CXR, an 8-billion-parameter vision–language model trained on four public datasets (MIMIC-CXR, CheXpert Plus, ReXGradient-160k and IU-Xray) by supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning (group-relative policy optimization) against a composite lexical, semantic and clinical-error reward. We evaluated held-out test sets and an external proprietary dataset, with RadCliQ as primary metric and expert radiologist validation. Here we show that our method improves report quality and generalization: UNIRG-CXR surpasses prior models on the ReXrank benchmark across four datasets and two generation settings, exceeding the previous best score by over 50% on two test sets, and produces fewer clinically significant errors while maintaining performance on unseen data sources and across demographic subgroups.

item.title: Latitude modulates climate-driven maize yield gains across the central U.S. “warming hole”
item.dc:creator: Nenghan Wan
Haidong Zhao
Jerry L. Hatfield
Roger A. Pielke
M. B. Kirkham
Stephen M. Welch
Lina Zhang
Zhijuan Liu
item.description:
Authors: Nenghan Wan, Haidong Zhao, Jerry L. Hatfield, Roger A. Pielke, M. B. Kirkham, Stephen M. Welch, Lina Zhang, Zhijuan Liu, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Maize yield responses to climate change differ seasonally and regionally, with both positive and negative impacts shaped by local climate trends and management decisions. Here, using a phenology-aligned moving crop-season framework and the Hybrid-Maize model (1991–2024) across five U.S. Corn Belt states, we quantify climate-driven yield contributions and show that they transition from southern declines to northern gains, reflecting the persistent influence of the central U.S. summer warming hole characterized by cooling maximum temperatures and increasing rainfall. A systematic thermal mismatch between environmental heat availability and hybrid growing degree day requirements is observed, particularly south of 42°N, where thermal matching declined despite favorable thermal conditions. Contrasting trends in thermal matching and reproductive duration help explain the latitude-dependent structure of climate-driven yield contributions. Our findings highlight how hybrid selection modulates the impacts of temperature, precipitation, vapor pressure deficit, and radiation trends on maize yield gains across the U.S. Corn Belt.

item.title: Thin-film lithium niobate waveguide-integrated p-i-n Tungsten selenide photodiodes with 10Gbit/s data reception
item.dc:creator: Weijia Tang
Zixian Wei
Ting He
Haoyu Huang
Xin He
Su Wu
Jun Liu
Changyuan Yu
item.description:
Authors: Weijia Tang, Zixian Wei, Ting He, Haoyu Huang, Xin He, Su Wu, Jun Liu, Changyuan Yu, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Thin-film lithium niobate (TFLN) is a promising photonic platform in next-generation integrated optoelectronics and on-chip/chip-chip interconnection due to its attractive optical property and versatility. However, integration of conventional-material-based photodetectors on TFLN platforms still faces multiple challenges. Herein, a high-bandwidth TFLN-based waveguide-integrated lateral WSe 2 p-i-n photodetector is presented. The localized self-aligned doping process eliminates slow carrier diffusion and defect trapping in doped regions which further boosts modulation bandwidth. Secondly, n-type and p-type Ohmic contacts, along with a high-quality p-n junction, are achieved through Se vacancy defect engineering and high-work function molybdenum oxide buffer layer, respectively. Furthermore, combined with the high dielectric constant of lithium niobate suppressing ionized impurity scattering, carrier mobilities exceeding 350 cm 2 /V·s are achieved for both electrons and holes, significantly accelerating carrier drift. The device features a measured bandwidth of 1.12 GHz and a data rate up to 10 Gbit/s in visible light. Separately, the device achieves a responsivity of ~492 mA·W −1 and a near-unity external quantum efficiency of 95.6% at 638 nm. This combination of two-dimensional homostructure and TFLN nano-waveguides provides a basis for high-speed photodetectors and visible-light interconnections in future TFLN integrated optoelectronics and optical input/output applications.

item.title: Structural basis of ligand-mediated transition to higher-order rubisco assemblies
item.dc:creator: Albert K. Liu
Benjamin Kaeser
Jose H. Pereira
Leah J. Taylor-Kearney
Michal Hammel
Eva Nogales
Paul D. Adams
Patrick M. Shih
item.description:
Authors: Albert K. Liu, Benjamin Kaeser, Jose H. Pereira, Leah J. Taylor-Kearney, Michal Hammel, Eva Nogales, Paul D. Adams, Patrick M. Shih
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Proteins often assemble as higher order complexes, underlying a diversity of molecular structures and biological functions. The emergence of protein-protein interactions between binding partners is generally considered to be the primary driver of oligomerization. However, ligand binding has also been demonstrated to affect higher-order assembly, though this phenomenon is not widely considered as a primary driver of oligomerization. Here, we describe the mechanism by which different rubisco oligomeric states are induced via ligand binding. By expanding the phylogenetic sampling of a unique clade of rubisco, we discover a range of oligomeric responses to ligand binding across the phylogeny and identify the structural features responsible for shifts in the oligomeric state that ultimately provide a path to evolving new quaternary structures. Here, we identify a ligand-dependent mechanism giving rise to new protein assemblies, in contrast with the typical process of evolving new protein-protein interfaces directly. Our findings describe a means by which binding and entrenchment of a ligand enables an increase in structural complexity.

item.title: Probing topological edge states in a molecular synthetic dimension
item.dc:creator: Adarsh P. Raghuram
Francesca M. Blondell
Jonathan M. Mortlock
Benjamin P. Maddox
Sohail Dasgupta
Holly A. J. Middleton-Spencer
Kaden R. A. Hazzard
Hannah M. Price
item.description:
Authors: Adarsh P. Raghuram, Francesca M. Blondell, Jonathan M. Mortlock, Benjamin P. Maddox, Sohail Dasgupta, Holly A. J. Middleton-Spencer, Kaden R. A. Hazzard, Hannah M. Price, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Synthetic dimensions, where additional spatial dimensions are encoded within the internal states of a quantum system, allow the realisation of phenomena usually inaccessible in experiments. Ultracold polar molecules are an ideal platform for synthetic dimensions, providing large Hilbert spaces of long-lived rotational and hyperfine states that can be linked with microwave fields to simulate tunnelling. Here, we realise a one-dimensional synthetic lattice using the rotational states of ultracold RbCs molecules and investigate the topological properties of the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model. We spectroscopically probe the system using an auxiliary rotational state and study the time dynamics after deterministic state preparation. We demonstrate long coherence times, reaching ~ 500 tunnelling periods even for lattices spanning eight rotational states. Using full site-resolved readout over long evolution times, we study the robustness of topologically protected edge states against perturbations that preserve or break chiral symmetry. These results establish ultracold molecules as a powerful platform for quantum simulation using synthetic dimensions.

item.title: Near-infrared plasmonic response in hyperdoped silicon nanoantennas for all-silicon photodetection
item.dc:creator: Rang Li
Yi Liu
Mohd Saif Shaikh
Xia Wang
Yordan Georgiev
Xiaoli Sun
Chi Pang
Kambiz Jamshidi
item.description:
Authors: Rang Li, Yi Liu, Mohd Saif Shaikh, Xia Wang, Yordan Georgiev, Xiaoli Sun, Chi Pang, Kambiz Jamshidi, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Plasmonic materials enable subwavelength confinement of light through the collective response of free carriers, but their operational spectral range is typically constrained by intrinsic carrier densities. Hyperdoped semiconductors offer a route to engineer plasmonic properties within a CMOS-compatible platform, yet their plasmonic response in silicon remains largely limited to the mid-infrared. Here we show that nanoantenna engineering extends the plasmonic response of phosphorus-hyperdoped silicon toward the near-infrared. The nanoantenna arrays exhibit tunable, polarization-dependent resonances in the 1–2 μm range, arising from geometry-driven localized modes on a Drude-like electronic background. Leveraging these effects, we realize all-silicon photoconductive detectors operating at 1.55 μm and room temperature, with a maximum bias-assisted responsivity of 0.58 A/W at 0.5 V. This response arises from plasmon-enhanced sub-bandgap absorption combined with trap-assisted photoconductive gain and therefore does not represent the intrinsic quantum efficiency. These results extend the spectral functionality of silicon photonics beyond its intrinsic absorption limits for integrated sensing, imaging, and optical communication.

item.title: UMIche: a UMI-centric analysis platform for enhancing molecular quantification accuracy in bulk and single-cell sequencing
item.dc:creator: Jianfeng Sun
Shuang Li
Stefan Canzar
Adam P. Cribbs
item.description:
Authors: Jianfeng Sun, Shuang Li, Stefan Canzar, Adam P. Cribbs
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Unique molecular identifiers (UMIs) are widely utilised in RNA-sequencing (RNA-seq) technologies to eliminate polymerase chain reaction (PCR) duplicates, thereby improving the accuracy of molecular quantification. However, synthesis errors in UMIs during sequencing often compromise the reliability of UMI counting. While various computational methods have been developed for error correction, the lack of a unified benchmarking and validation framework impedes systematic evaluation and optimisation. Here, we present UMIche, an open-source, UMI-centric computational platform designed to enhance UMI-assisted molecular quantification. Its application to collapsing monomer and homotrimer UMIs across multiple bulk and single-cell sequencing protocols demonstrates effective PCR-duplicate removal. Across a broad spectrum of simulated and experimental datasets with ground truth, most UMI collapsing methods integrated into UMIche perform similarly under low-error conditions, whereas set-cover optimisation and majority voting show greater robustness as the UMI error profile becomes more pronounced. Together, these capabilities enable scalable UMI collapsing, systematic benchmarking, and method development to improve molecular quantification.

item.title: Low-thermal-budget solution-processed montmorillonite dielectric for low-voltage 2D electronics
item.dc:creator: Wenjie Li
Junying Xue
Peng Chen
Yongping Dai
Jing He
Ruihao Tan
Jifeng Ge
Tingyi Xia
item.description:
Authors: Wenjie Li, Junying Xue, Peng Chen, Yongping Dai, Jing He, Ruihao Tan, Jifeng Ge, Tingyi Xia, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Low-voltage and high-performance electronic devices based on two-dimensional (2D) semiconductors demand high-quality dielectrics with efficient capacitive gating. However, it currently relies on specially engineered atomic layer deposition (ALD) of ultrathin high- k HfO 2 and ZrO 2 , or high-temperature vapor-phase growth of 2D dielectrics with post-growth transfer process. Here, we report a facile solution-processed 2D dielectric with an ultra-low thermal budget (i.e., at room temperature), while delivering competitive device metrics (e.g., low operating voltage and small hysteresis). This is enabled by an organic-free colloidal ink of montmorillonite (MTM) in environmentally friendly water solvent, eliminating the need for organic ligands or surfactants and thus the post-deposition high-temperature thermal annealing. Specifically, all-solution-processed MoS 2 field-effect transistors with MTM dielectric exhibit a low operating voltage of 1 V and small hysteresis (down to 1 mV). The solution process is generally compatible with diverse n-type and p-type 2D semiconductors such as MoS 2 , MoSe 2 and WSe 2 . Moreover, the robust and reproducible MTM dielectric enables scalable device integration into logic circuits, including inverters, AND, NOR, and NAND gates, as well as static random-access memory (SRAM). The scalable room-temperature solution-processed 2D dielectric offers a route to all-solution-processed and low-voltage 2D electronics.

item.title: High-pressure synthesis of a polymeric N3H2 solid stabilized by hydrogen bonds
item.dc:creator: Umbertoluca Ranieri
Grégory Geneste
Gunnar Weck
Sarah Bolton
James Spender
Akun Liang
Bernhard Massani
Gaston Garbarino
item.description:
Authors: Umbertoluca Ranieri, Grégory Geneste, Gunnar Weck, Sarah Bolton, James Spender, Akun Liang, Bernhard Massani, Gaston Garbarino, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Polymeric nitrogen represents a long-sought class of high energy density materials, in which single-bonded nitrogen networks release large amounts of energy upon decomposition to molecular N 2 . However, polymeric nitrogen allotropes require extreme pressures to synthesize and cannot be recovered at ambient conditions due to surface instabilities. Hydrogen has been proposed as a key element to stabilize such frameworks, yet polymeric nitrogen–hydrogen solids have until now remained the realm of theoretical calculations. Here, we report the high-pressure synthesis of polymeric N 3 H 2 at 134(3)–139(1) GPa from N 2 –H 2 mixtures. Synchrotron single-crystal X-ray diffraction, Raman spectroscopy and first-principles calculations reveal a fully single-bonded framework of 1-dimensional chains of N 6 rings, each decorated by four H atoms. The chains of N 6 H 4 units are cross-linked through hydrogen bonds. Employing modern synchrotron sources, hydrogen positions are directly resolved from diffraction data at 139(1) GPa. At ambient conditions, N 3 H 2 exhibits an estimated energy of decomposition of 7.98 kJ/g, highlighting hydrogen-stabilized polymeric nitrogen as a promising class of energetic materials.

item.title: Experience modifies the synaptome architecture in the developing and adult mouse brain
item.dc:creator: Hanan Woods
Ülkü Günar
Sarah Catherine Gillard
Beverley Notman
Kunhao Yuan
Digin Dominic
Emily Robson
Gabor Varga
item.description:
Authors: Hanan Woods, Ülkü Günar, Sarah Catherine Gillard, Beverley Notman, Kunhao Yuan, Digin Dominic, Emily Robson, Gabor Varga, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 11204
Abstract: Abstract Synaptome architecture describes the spatiotemporal distribution of highly diverse excitatory synapses throughout the brain. Whether and how this architecture is impacted by experience and sensory input is unknown. We found that environmental enrichment and monocular visual deprivation drive large-scale reconfiguration of excitatory synapse populations in more than one hundred regions of the mouse brain. Different experiences modify distinct subsets of synapse types and subtypes, with patterns aligned with protein turnover rates and connectome architecture. Similarity in experience-dependent reconfiguration during development and adulthood indicates shared mechanisms of synaptome adaptation across the lifespan. Our findings support a population-selection model in which experiences drive adaptation by selectively modifying synapse types and subtypes distributed across the brain. Experience-driven reconfiguration of synaptome architecture shares features with the response to aging, sleep deprivation, brain injury and genetic mutations, supporting a unifying principle of brain adaptation.

item.title: Switchable nucleophile-electrophile chemistry enables functional four-electron Li-I2 batteries
item.dc:creator: Lei Huang
Zhehan Yi
Tao Xiao
Jin-Lin Yang
Zefang Yang
Yiren Cheng
Shixing Yuan
Wulong Li
item.description:
Authors: Lei Huang, Zhehan Yi, Tao Xiao, Jin-Lin Yang, Zefang Yang, Yiren Cheng, Shixing Yuan, Wulong Li, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Four-electron iodine redox chemistry offers a high theoretical specific energy of ~1324 Wh kgI −1 , yet its practical realization is fundamentally limited by the conflicting demands of rapid I 0 /I + oxidation, effective suppression of iodine shuttling, and stabilization of highly reactive I + species. Here we report a redox-active, Lewis acid/base-tunable phthalimide that resolves these constraints through a single-molecule polarity-switching mechanism. Upon electrochemical oxidation, electrophilic phthalimide δ+ strongly interacts with nucleophilic iodine and polyiodide species, concurrently suppressing polyiodide shuttling and promoting their conversion to I + . The consecutively generated phthalimide δ− acts as a nucleophilic stabilizer for the resulting I + species. This electrochemically driven polarity switching of phthalimide enables flexible four-electron Li-I 2 pouch cells that deliver ~400 mAh gI −1 capacity, a specific energy exceeding 1200 Wh kgI −1 , a high cathode-level specific energy ( ~ 883.4 Wh kg(cathode) −1 ), and stable cycling over 1000 cycles. The successful integration of these cells into wearable wireless charging and motion-sensing systems demonstrates the potential of polarity-switchable iodine chemistry for next-generation flexible energy-storage devices.

Abstract: Abstract This phase Ib/II investigator-initiated, open label trial aims to show the safety and efficacy of Cystadane (betaine) in aspartylglucosaminuria, a lysosomal storage disorder characterized by progressive cognitive decline, in Finnish patients homozygous for the Finnish major mutation, aged between 3 and 17 years at study begin (recruited: 25, analyzed: 21). Oral Cystadane efficacy and safety were studied over 48 months. The primary endpoint of the study, reduction of glycoasparagines in the urine, was quantitatively determined using liquid chromatography/mass spectrometry and normalized to urine creatinine. Urine glycoasparagines are significantly reduced upon Cystadane treatment (by 68.6% ±10.8%; p = 0.000), and the study thus meets its primary endpoint. Our data show that Cystadane/betaine efficiently improves the main disease biomarker, and it is safe to use in aspartylglucosaminuria. Further studies should be carried out in a larger patient population over a longer time to demonstrate the effects on disease progression. EudraCT registration number 2017-000645-48.

item.title: Single photon reflection from a quantum dot in a waveguide
item.dc:creator: Tarun Patel
Matteo Pennacchietti
Sayan Gangopadhyay
Dan Dalacu
Philip J. Poole
Stephen Hughes
Michael E. Reimer
item.description:
Authors: Tarun Patel, Matteo Pennacchietti, Sayan Gangopadhyay, Dan Dalacu, Philip J. Poole, Stephen Hughes, Michael E. Reimer
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Single-atom waveguide-QED systems have emerged as a leading platform for demonstrating non-linear optics in the few-photon regime. Devices with such non-linear behavior are necessary for developing deterministic gates for photonic quantum computing. Artificial atoms coupled to nanophotonic or superconducting waveguides can be used to engineer highly efficient light-matter interfaces for such non-linear interactions, where every photon in the system interacts with the quantum emitter. However, it has been a challenge to access the reflection port of the waveguide due to the inability of rejecting stray electromagnetic fields that do not interact with the artificial atom. Here, we show coherent reflection of single photons from a semiconductor quantum dot strongly coupled to the fundamental waveguide mode of a nanowire. We utilize the tapered end of the nanowire for ideal mode-matching in a vertical geometry, enabled by the extinction technique developed. This mode-matching allows for efficient transfer of photons from the input to the reflection port while having all interacted with the quantum dot. Such a high-efficiency scalable photonic platform opens up applications in few-photon quantum nonlinear optics and has been proposed for creating key resource states for universal photon-based quantum computing.

Authors: Renuka Dahiya, Chihyean Ong, Gigani Dharshan, Megan M. Barry, Cheyenne A. Ernst, Minhyung Kim, Jin Wu, Vasanta Putluri, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Bone metastasis is the major cause of morbidity and mortality in advanced prostate cancer, yet current therapies provide only limited clinical benefit. Here, we show that prostate cancer cells metabolically adapt to the bone microenvironment by utilizing bone-cell-derived lactate as an alternative nutrient source. Beyond fueling oxidative phosphorylation, lactate serves as carbon source for fatty acid synthesis. Among the resulting lipid products, oleic acid is secreted to reward osteoblast, establishing a reciprocal metabolic interplay that supports both tumor progression and pathological bone formation. Mechanistically, we identify MCT1 as the essential transporter mediating lactate uptake in bone-colonizing tumor cells. MCT1 expression is coordinately regulated by NFAT signaling and extracellular glucose availability at both transcriptional and post-translational levels. Genetic deletion and pharmacological inhibition of MCT1 markedly suppresses prostate tumor growth in bone. Together, these findings uncover a lactate-driven metabolic crosstalk, identifying MCT1 as a promising therapeutic target for prostate cancer bone metastasis.

Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 11455
Abstract: Abstract Antarctic Bottom Water (AABW) is decreasing in volume due to climate change with potential consequences for abyssal carbon storage, where carbon is locked away from the atmosphere for centuries. Understanding the formation and export of dissolved organic matter (DOM) on the Antarctic shelf is therefore essential to determine how organic carbon enters this deep-sea reservoir. Here, we investigate solid-phase extractable DOM (SPE-DOM) transformations in the Weddell Sea, where half of AABW forms. Molecular and structural properties of SPE-DOM remain unchanged during dense-water formation. Shelf processes minimally affect exported organics into the deep-sea, likely due to remineralization to inorganic carbon enhanced by long residence times on the shelf. Consequently, the dominant SPE-DOM signature in Weddell Sea Deep Water (WSDW) is established before dense shelf waters mix with warmer off-shelf waters. We estimate that 0.155 ± 0.03 PgC are transferred annually from the Weddell Sea to AABW, and that its molecular composition is expected to remain conserved despite ongoing climate-driven weakening of AABW.

Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 11165
Abstract: Abstract Temporal dynamics of psychiatric symptoms challenge researchers and clinicians due to their inherent unpredictability. The cyclical on–off nature of symptoms linked to physiological rhythms, such as the menstrual cycle, provides a unique window to apply temporal and dynamic modeling of psychiatric symptoms. This can be studied in premenstrual dysphoric disorder, a female hormone-triggered condition characterized by cyclical symptoms. Yet intra-individual temporal patterns and dynamics of these symptoms remain unknown. Here we show that individuals with premenstrual dysphoric disorder differ widely in symptom timing, severity, and persistence, clustering into distinct temporal symptom profiles. Dynamic modelling uncovers temporal order among core psychiatric symptoms, with anxiety emerging as a central symptom in the unfolding of affective dysregulation. Depression shows the strongest predictive associations with subsequent severity of the other core symptoms, while irritability predicts the severity of depression at the longest time-interval. These temporal symptom dynamics reveal mechanistic psychoneuroendocrine pathways and inform precision, time-sensitive interventions for the mental health of individuals with premenstrual dysphoric disorder.

item.title: The representational geometry of cognitive maps under cognitive control
item.dc:creator: Seongmin A. Park

item.description:
Authors: Seongmin A. Park, Maryam Zolfaghar, Jacob Russin, Douglas S. Miller, Randall C. O’Reilly, Erie D. Boorman
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Recent work has shown that the brain abstracts non-spatial relationships between entities or task states into representations called cognitive maps. Here, we investigate how cognitive control enables flexible top-down selection of goal-relevant information from multidimensional cognitive maps retrieved from memory. We examine the relationship between cognitive control and representational geometry by conducting parallel analyses of functional magnetic resonance imaging data and recurrent neural network models trained to perform the same task. We find both stable map-like representations in a medial temporal lobe and orbitofrontal cortical network that reflect both task-relevant and irrelevant dimensions and context-dependent, orthogonal representations of only task-relevant dimensions in a frontoparietal network. These representational motifs also emerge with distinct temporal profiles over the course of training in the recurrent neural network, with map-like representations appearing first. We further show that increasing control demands due to incongruence (conflicting responses) between current task-relevant and irrelevant dimensions impact the geometry of subjective representations, and the degree of this effect further accounts for individual differences in cognitive control. Taken together, our findings show how complementary representational geometries balance stability and behavioral flexibility, and reveal an intricate relationship between cognitive control and cognitive map geometry.

Abstract: Abstract Tumour-promoting inflammation and immune evasion are key features of cancer, but prospective evidence linking specific immune pathways to prostate cancer risk remains limited. Here we show that circulating proteins involved in immune regulation may influence prostate cancer development. We analyse 368 immune- and inflammation-related proteins measured in blood samples from men in the European Prospective Investigation into Cancer and Nutrition (EPIC), including 1434 cases and matched controls, and combine these results with data from UK Biobank. While no proteins are associated with risk in EPIC alone after multiple testing correction, meta-analysis identifies several proteins linked to prostate cancer risk, including IL15 and FLT3LG, in particular, in blood taken long before diagnosis. Higher levels of immune surveillance-related proteins, particularly those involved in natural killer and T cell activity, are associated with lower prostate cancer risk, whereas genetic evidence implicates PARP1, SPINT2 and NME3 in increased risk. These findings suggest that immune pathways play a role in prostate cancer development and highlight potential targets for prevention.

Abstract: Abstract The transcription factor TATA-box-binding protein (TBP) plays a crucial role in neurons, as highlighted by its involvement in spinocerebellar ataxia type 17 (SCA17), where pathological polyglutamine expansions disrupt its function. While the molecular pathomechanisms remain unclear, our previous study showed that calcium-activated calpains cleave TBP in SCA17 cell and animal models. Here, we pinpoint a major calpain cleavage site after residue T106, C-terminal to TBP’s polyglutamine tract. The resulting polyglutamine-containing N-terminal fragments mislocalise to the cytoplasm and exhibit increased aggregation. Both the N-terminal and the nuclear-localised C-terminal fragments contribute to calpain overactivation. SCA17 cell line-based multi-omics analyses revealed that TBP fragments alter pathways linked to neuronal function and neurodegeneration, identifying AMOT as a key player. Further analyses in SCA17 cell lines, patient-derived fibroblasts and induced neurons as well as in rat and zebrafish models confirmed AMOT’s pivotal role in neurons, regulated by TBP and mediated via YAP1-dependent signalling. These findings offer further insights into TBP’s neuronal function and suggest broader implications of AMOT for neurodegenerative and neurodevelopmental disorders.

item.title: Two functionally distinct amyloid-β intermediates link aggregation pathways to pathology in Alzheimer’s disease

Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 11333
Abstract: Abstract Neurotoxic intermediates formed during amyloid-β (Aβ) aggregation are thought to drive Alzheimer’s disease, yet their rarity and transient nature have obscured their identity and formation pathways in the human brain. Here, we combine super-resolution microscopy and single-molecule functional imaging with kinetic modelling to classify Aβ intermediates according to their membrane-disrupting activity and connect their damaging effects to the aggregation pathways that generate them. Applying this framework to recombinant Aβ42, an Alzheimer’s knock-in mouse model and human Alzheimer’s brain tissue, we find two functionally distinct intermediate populations present across all systems. They form through separate aggregation routes and differ in their neurotoxicity, abundance and susceptibility to inhibition. Both damage neurons and glia, but only one converts into plaques. Suppressing these intermediates pharmacologically in mice reduces plaque burden, attenuates astrogliosis and improves cognition. Our findings connect model systems with human pathology and identify intermediate formation pathways as actionable therapeutic targets across protein-misfolding disorders.

Authors: Adithya V. Madduri, Randall J. Ellis, Chirag M. Lakhani, David A. Bennett, Chirag J. Patel
Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 11124
Abstract: Abstract Univariate differential expression analysis dominates single-cell transcriptomic studies of Alzheimer’s disease, yet marginal testing alone cannot resolve multivariate disease-associated structure or distinguish clinical from neuropathological signatures. Here we introduce TriSCOPE, a framework integrating multivariate predictive modeling, donor-aware differential expression, and pseudotime inference, applied to six Alzheimer’s disease snRNA-seq datasets comprising ~4.2 million nuclei from 627 donors. Across six major brain cell types and 41 subclusters, we identify cell-type-specific predictively expressed genes that are largely non-overlapping with differentially expressed genes, revealing disease-relevant signals invisible to univariate approaches. Conditional GWAS–eQTL colocalization anchors a subset of these predictively expressed genes to inherited Alzheimer’s disease risk loci, including 27 genetically supported gene–cell type pairs (among them ARL17B , JAZF1 ) with no significant differential expression. Integration across all three analytical branches nominates high-confidence convergent programs including astrocytic stress markers (such as GFAP , MT2A ), neuronal signaling genes (like RASGEF1B , LINGO1 , NRG1 ), and microglial and oligodendrocyte regulators (including SYTL3 , SPP1 , APOD ). Comparison of clinical and neuropathological models reveals cell-type-specific divergence between cognitive and pathological Alzheimer’s disease signatures. Key predictively expressed genes including ARL17B , LINGO1 , and APOE replicate across independent cohorts, with cross-cohort generalizability confirmed across all three analytical branches of TriSCOPE.

Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 10450
Abstract: Abstract Sea-level reconstructions and numerical models suggest that the vulnerable West Antarctic Ice Sheet underwent major mass losses during the late Pleistocene, raising global sea level by several metres. However, direct evidence from ice-sheet proximal records for such retreat has remained inconclusive. Here we investigate variations in clay mineral assemblages and past ocean temperatures archived in West Antarctic continental margin sediments during the last 800,000 years. Our results demonstrate that the supply of glacigenic detritus sourced from the main outlet glaciers in the Amundsen Sea sector of the West Antarctic Ice Sheet ceased almost entirely during all previous warm periods, documenting the loss of their drainage basins. Concomitant seawater warming, revealed by a microfossil proxy, is attributed to intensified deep-water advection towards Antarctica’s Pacific margin, which is corroborated by the clay mineralogical evidence. Our findings show that ocean forcing can drive major deglaciation of West Antarctica and related global sea-level rise.

Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 11117
Abstract: Abstract Anaerobic methanotrophic (ANME) archaea are key regulators of methane emissions in anoxic environments, yet their physiology remains poorly understood due to the lack of axenic cultures. Here, we show that cultivation on poised electrodes yields near-axenic cultures (95.8% relative abundance) of a freshwater ANME, for which we propose the name ‘ Candidatus Methanoperedens vercellensis’. We identified key physiological properties of ‘ Ca . M. vercellensis’: doubling times of 4.6 days at 30 °C, menaquinone as respiratory electron carrier, the inability to oxidize ethane, and preferential reduction of iron oxides over nitrate after cultivation on electrodes. A 3.3 Å cryo-electron microscopy structure of filaments displayed on the archaeal surface revealed polymerized OmcZ-type cytochrome nanowires, which are homologous to OmcZ nanowires essential for long-range (>10 μm) extracellular electron transfer (EET) in Geobacter sulfurreducens . The archaeal OmcZ-type nanowires include dense, collinear stacking of protected hemesakin to bacterial OmcZ nanowires, but with post-translational modification, thus yielding morphology distinct from bacterial OmcZ nanowires. Notably, in contrast to bacterial OmcZ, archaeal OmcZ-type nanowires do not form interconnected networks, and hemes are less solvent-exposed, which can protect them from the environment. Surprisingly, these archaea assemble OmcZ into nanowires even in the apparent absence of prolyl isomerase involved in folding bacterial OmcZ. This work establishes a model system for molecular understanding of nanowire-mediated EET in archaea.

Abstract: Abstract Digital infrastructure is crucial for economic opportunities, social inclusion, and civic participation, but benefits remain unevenly distributed. The findings call for interventions that complement infrastructure access with support for technology use and skills development. The resulting indices are publicly available to support future research on digital inequality.

Abstract: Abstract Arc andesites are hybrids generated by mixing of mafic and silicic magmas. The silicic endmember can contribute to crustal growth or trigger explosive eruptions, yet remains difficult to constrain due to limited representation in the erupted record. Here, we show that textural, elemental and isotopic records preserved in plagioclase can distinguish between trapped and erupted crystal mush, thus constraining conditions of magma storage vs. eruption in arc systems. We define the plagioclase eruptibility field, a narrow and recurrent anorthite range (An~61) that represents erupted melt across Central Andes volcanoes upon mafic recharge. The recycled plagioclase cargo is dominantly An~43, recording prolonged crystallisation and assimilation within silicic mushes. This pattern repeats in continental and composite arcs globally, indicating strong eruptive filtering of arc magmas and widespread occurrence of dormant felsic and mafic mushes that, in most cases, contribute to crustal growth; yet exceptionally, felsic mushes can rapidly remobilise to generate super-eruptions.

Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 11327
Abstract: Abstract Collective memory shapes how societies respond to extreme climate events, yet long-term evidence on how the collective memory of such events becomes perceptually biased over time is lacking. Here, we utilise four centuries (1470–1900) of climatic archives from northern China, along with tree–ring–based hydroclimate reconstructions, which are validated against instrumental observations of Wet/Dry Index (1901–2000) to fill the gap. We find that historical records reveal systematic, non-random mismatches, where severity assessments are often biased toward recent experience rather than absolute climatic anomalies. Correlations between historical and natural records increase when the natural series is re-standardised using 20–40-year sliding windows, reflecting a generational offset. A heuristic agent-based model reproduces this pattern, suggesting that generational amnesia is sufficient to explain the offsets in perception of environmental change. We argue that historical archives carry a generational imprint of perceptual bias, in which the severity of climate extremes is judged against recent lived experience rather than long-term climate variability. This has implications for bias-aware corrections for risk assessment, adaptation, and paleoclimate reconstruction.

It also enabled imaging of Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Acinetobacter baumannii outer membranes, which lack the characteristic protein trimers observed in model E. coli . Finally, we discovered growth-phase dependent alterations in E. coli pole morphology, where trimer networks typical of exponential-phase cells were unresolved and morphological defects appeared.

item.title: Topological Josephson trijunctions as a Majorana source and path
item.dc:creator: Kyungtae Kim
June-Young M. Lee
Hyeongseop Kim
H.-S. Sim
item.description:
Authors: Kyungtae Kim, June-Young M. Lee, Hyeongseop Kim, H.-S. Sim
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Majorana bound states (MBSs) are zero-energy localized states in topological superconductors, obeying non-Abelian braiding statistics. Manipulation of mobile MBSs, encompassing their on-demand generation, propagation, and fusion, is essential for braiding MBSs and operating topological qubits. We show that the manipulation is enabled by a trijunction formed on a topological insulator in a perpendicular magnetic field, where three Josephson junctions meet. While the superconducting phases at the trijunction center evolve to cross a boundary between topological and non-topological phase domains, the trijunction offers two distinct dynamics, source/sink and path, depending on the phase boundaries. At a source/sink boundary, two MBSs are pairwise generated at the center, and one of them is ejected to a Josephson junction. The reverse, pair annihilation by collision of two MBSs, can also happen. At a path boundary, an MBS moves from a Josephson junction to the trijunction center or vice versa, without involving other MBSs. Exploiting the two dynamics, fusion and braiding of MBSs can be operated in a trijunction network. We illustrate this with a double trijunction setup, where non-Abelian state evolutions associated with MBSs can be manipulated without dynamical control of the setup and detected by Josephson emission spectroscopy.

item.title: Antagonistic second-messenger signalling coordinates Pseudomonas aeruginosa surface colonization and virulence
item.dc:creator: Maya Bruderer
Jiangning Li
Andreas Kaczmarczyk
Simon van Vliet

Rao Rohan Girish

item.description:
Authors: Maya Bruderer, Jiangning Li, Andreas Kaczmarczyk, Simon van Vliet, Kai Schleicher, Rao Rohan Girish, Pablo Manfredi, Nicole Thürkauf, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Efficient colonisation of host tissue surfaces is a prerequisite for bacterial infection. In the human pathogen Pseudomonas aeruginosa , the second messengers cAMP and c-di-GMP regulate surface behaviours and virulence, but how these pathways are coordinated during tissue infection has remained unclear. Here we demonstrate that cAMP and c-di-GMP establish mutually exclusive signalling states at the single-cell level, generating distinct subpopulations of motile and surface-attached cells through pathway-specific control of type IV pili (T4P). Initial surface contact triggers an increase in c-di-GMP, activating FimW and driving stable attachment via bipolar T4P formation. This state is progressively replaced by cAMP, which inactivates FimW-dependent attachment and induces FimX-mediated T4P polarisation, surface motility and virulence activation. The resulting signalling transition enforces coexisting subpopulations, with attached cells gradually displaced by spreading cells. Using a human airway tissue model, we show that both T4P-mediated adhesion and twitching motility are required for invasion and tissue damage. Based on this, we propose that reciprocal cAMP–c-di-GMP signalling coordinates complementary T4P functions to optimise P. aeruginosa surface colonisation and infection.

item.dc:creator: Uwe Langenmayr
Julia Schuler
Viktor Slednev
Wolf Fichtner
item.description:
Authors: Uwe Langenmayr, Julia Schuler, Viktor Slednev, Wolf Fichtner
Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 11500
Abstract: Abstract Synthetic energy carriers can connect renewable-energy-rich potential production regions with distant demand centers, but the emergence of trade depends on total supply costs. Here, we develop a spatially resolved heuristic combining hydrogen production costs with ports, pipelines, and shipping routes, as well as syntheses, cracking, and reformation processes, to identify key import corridors. Across 10,883 production locations and seven different scenarios, we find that export regions connected to the importer through retrofit-ready pipelines remain competitive despite only moderate renewable potentials. Meanwhile, for remote exporters competitiveness depends on port availability and coastal access through pipeline networks. Gaseous hydrogen dominates short pipeline routes, and ammonia is preferred for maritime trade, whereas methanol and methane emerge in long multimodal chains. Additional results show that low-cost heat availability is required for the competitiveness of liquid organic hydrogen carriers, while accounting for market values of conventional counterparts boosts ammonia and methanol trade.

item.description:
Authors: Gabriel Britto Monteiro, Christopher Perrella, Sarah K. Scholten, Morgan Facchin, Andre N. Luiten, Graham D. Bruce, Kishan Dholakia
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Laser speckle, the granular intensity pattern arising from random optical interference, provides a high-dimensional encoding of spectral information that can be exploited for precision metrology. Speckle-based spectrometers have advanced rapidly owing to their compact footprint, mechanical robustness and alignment agnostic nature, yet their spectral resolution has remained limited to the picometre scale. In this work, we break this limit by employing an integrating sphere as a multiply scattering cavity with access to a high range of path lengths to enhance spectral sensitivity. At 780 nm, the resulting device achieves a resolution of 6 fm, corresponding to a resolving power of 1.3 × 10 8 , representing an approximately 80-fold improvement over previous implementations. This ultra-high resolution enables clear discrimination of laser sidebands generated by an electro-optical modulator, with extracted sideband powers agreeing with expected values to within 1%. It further permits a direct speckle-based measurement of the hyperfine structure of the D 2 transition in 85 Rb, with transmission spectra differing by no more than 3.7% from independent wavemeter-referenced measurements. These results establish speckle as a platform for ultra-high precision spectroscopy, radio-frequency spectrometry, and microwave photonics.

Abstract: Abstract Exploiting thin Li foils ≤ 20 μm is required for high-energy-density and long-cycling-lifespan battery, but is severely hindered by the poor processability of Li, as well as its inhomogeneous plating behaviors and resulting low Coulombic efficiency. Abstract: Abstract Error recognition is fundamental to adaptive behavior, enabling rapid compensatory action when outcomes deviate from expectations. Frontoinsular recording sites were found to preferentially encode error-related activity, while centroparietal responses were intermixed with compensatory motor signals, making the former a compelling target for real-time error correction. Together, our findings demonstrate a human intracranial BCI harnessing insular brain activity, integrating cognitive processes directly into device control.

Abstract: Abstract Perovskite light-emitting diodes (PeLEDs) offer exceptional colour purity and efficiency for next-generation display applications. Despite the recent advances in device stability, achieving long-term stable PeLEDs under display-relevant conditions remains a critical challenge. The actual device half-life (T 50 ) experimentally measured for visible PeLEDs were in most cases limited to below 1000 h for any given brightness, in contrast to the much longer extrapolated lifetimes reported. The accumulated photon output of our PeLEDs over the course of their T 50 lifespan is found to sharply increase as the driving voltage drops to sub-bandgap values, highlighting the critical role of employing low-voltage device architectures in reaching the 1350-h/1000-nit stability milestone. Finally, a flexible active-matrix PeLED display prototype is developed, showing the potential of the devices for wearable optoelectronics.

Abstract: Abstract Associative memory, traditionally modeled by Hopfield networks, enables the retrieval of previously stored patterns from partial or noisy cues. Yet, the local computational principles which are required to enable this function remain incompletely understood. To formally characterize the local information processing in such systems, we employ a recent extension of information theory—Partial Information Decomposition. It decomposes the contribution of different inputs to an output into unique information from each input, redundant information across inputs, and synergistic information that emerges from combining different inputs. Applying this framework to individual neurons in classical Hopfield networks we find that below the memory capacity, the information in a neuron’s activity is characterized by high redundancy between the external pattern input and the internal recurrent input, while synergy and unique information are close to zero until the memory capacity is surpassed and performance drops steeply. Inspired by this observation, we use redundancy maximization at each neuron as an information-theoretic learning goal. This increases the network’s memory capacity to 1.59, a more than tenfold improvement over the 0.14 capacity of classical Hopfield networks, and also outperforming recent state-of-the-art implementations of Hopfield networks. Overall, this work establishes redundancy maximization as a design principle for associative memories and opens pathways for new associative memory models based on information-theoretic goals.

Abstract: Abstract The B cells of the human immune system have evolved somatic hypermutation (SHM) mechanisms that introduce mutations at the immunoglobulin genomic loci at a significantly higher frequency than the rest of the genome thereby allowing them to evolve antibody sequences without compromising fitness due to genome-wide mutations. Inspired by these observations, here we develop a continuous directed evolution platform in human B cell lines (CODE-HB) that repurposes the SHM mechanisms to a stable, non-immunoglobulin genomic locus of the human B cell lines to continuously evolve cytosolic and surface displayed proteins with a broad mutational spectrum comprising of substitutions, deletions and insertions. Using our human B cell surface display platform and CODE-HB, we evolve neutralizing antibodies targeting avian influenza and escape variants of influenza. Given the modularity and simplicity of CODE-HB, we anticipate that this platform can be used for rapidly evolving biotechnologically relevant biomolecules directly in human cells.

item.description:
Authors: Taylor Smith, Andreas Morr, Christof Schötz, Niklas Boers
Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 11286
Abstract: Abstract A wide body of work has applied the concept of critical slowing down to estimate the stability of different Earth system components. Most of them – such as global vegetation – are inherently non-stationary, for example due to strong seasonal forcing that complicates the estimation of their resilience to external perturbations. Here, we introduce a method to account for non-stationarity in estimating the resilience of diverse synthetic and real-world systems via a regression-based formulation of the Langevin equation. Our method does not require extensive data pre-processing, is robust to gaps in the data record, and does not require regular time sampling. We further show that our method can incorporate time-varying data uncertainties, derive uncertainty bounds for stability estimates, and can be natively extended to examine spatial systems. Our method is a drop-in replacement for widely-used autocorrelation-based resilience estimates, and can be applied across diverse Earth system components.
